title: What if?
cando: talk about plans that depend on something, and give advice

about.text: In this lesson you talk about plans that depend on something, like the weather or the money you have. You make a plan B for an event, read simple hire terms and a repair card, and give a friend advice about their plans.
goals: Talk about plans that depend on something: If it rains, we'll move to the café.
Use unless, as long as and as soon as: I'll ring them as soon as I get home.
Give advice with should, ought to, needn't and If I were you.
Read simple hire terms and a repair card, and write your plan with a plan B.
Plan an event with a backup plan, and give a friend advice about theirs.

chapters.title: Plan B
chapters.text:
In this lesson, you make plans that depend on something, and you give advice.
First, you listen to Mei. She's organising a leaving party for a colleague, Samir. She wants an outdoor party in the park. But what if it rains? Mei hasn't got a plan B, and she's stressed.
Her friend Carlos gives her advice. Listen to how he does it. He doesn't say: Do this. He says: If I were you, I'd book a backup venue. And: You should book it in advance.
Listen for three useful phrases: as long as, as soon as, and just to be on the safe side.

chapters.title: If it rains, we'll …
chapters.text:
There are two grammar points in this lesson.
The first is plans that depend on something. If it rains, we'll move to the café. The if half is in the present: if it rains. The other half has will: we'll move.
Don't put will in the if half. Say: if it rains. Not: if it will rain.
The same is true after unless, as long as and as soon as. I'll ring the café as soon as I get home. Not: as soon as I will get home.
Unless means if not. Unless it rains, we'll eat outside.
As long as means only if. They won't charge for the room as long as everyone orders food.
The second point is advice. You should book early. You ought to warn people. Should and ought to mean the same. Ought needs to after it. Should doesn't.
Needn't means it isn't necessary. You needn't buy all the food.

chapters.title: Hire terms and a repair card
chapters.text:
Next, you read two short documents.
The first is the terms and conditions of a party hire company. Read the small words carefully: as long as, unless, otherwise. That is where the money is. When are the things due back? What happens if you're late? How do you get your deposit back?
The second is a repair card from a community hall. The lift is out of order. The card tells you how to report a fault, and what happens next.
Then you write your own plan for an event, and what you'll do if something goes wrong.

chapters.title: Plan A and plan B
chapters.text:
In the task, you plan an event: a party, a family day out or a small concert. You have a budget, and you need a plan B.
First, tell your partner your plan. Say what you'll do if something goes wrong.
Then listen to your partner's plan and give advice. If I were you, I'd … You ought to … You needn't …
Good advice is short, clear and kind. And it gives a reason.

chapters.title: The book
chapters.text:
Last, you read a story from the Library about a plan that goes wrong.
Read it once for the story. Then read it again, and think: what would you advise the people in it?

warmup.prompt: You're planning a picnic with friends, and the forecast says rain. What do you do?
warmup.note: There is no wrong answer. Each one is a plan B. In this lesson, you learn to talk about plans that depend on something, and to give advice.

conversation.title: What will you do if it rains?
conversation.setting: Mei is organising a leaving party for her colleague Samir. After work, she talks to her friend Carlos about it.
lines: Carlos
You look stressed, Mei. Is everything OK?
Mei
Not really. I'm organising Samir's leaving party on Saturday, and I want it to be an outdoor party in Riverside Park.
Carlos
Sounds lovely. But what will you do if it rains?
Mei
That's the problem. I haven't got a plan B. What would you advise?
Carlos
If I were you, I'd book a backup venue, just to be on the safe side. The café by the park has a big room upstairs.
Mei
Isn't that expensive? My budget is only two hundred pounds.
Carlos
They won't charge for the room as long as everyone orders food. But you should book it in advance. It gets busy at weekends.
Mei
OK. And when do I decide? I can't wait until Saturday morning.
Carlos
Check the forecast on Friday. If it's dry, go ahead with the park. If it looks bad, move to the café.
Mei
That's sensible. I'll ring the café as soon as I get home.
Carlos
One more tip. You ought to warn everyone that there's a possibility of a change.
Mei
Good idea. And do I need to buy all the food myself?
Carlos
No, you needn't do that. Ask everyone to bring something. You'll cope, don't worry.
Mei
Thanks, Carlos. I feel much better now.

questions.a: She hasn't got a plan B if it rains.
wrong: She hasn't got any money for the party.
questions.why: Mei says: I haven't got a plan B.

questions.q: When will the café give Mei the room for free?
questions.a: as long as everyone orders food
wrong: if Mei books it on the day
questions.why: Carlos says: They won't charge for the room as long as everyone orders food.

questions.q: When will Mei decide between the park and the café?
questions.a: on Friday, after she checks the forecast
wrong: tonight, as soon as she gets home
questions.why: Carlos tells her to check the forecast on Friday and decide then.

phrases.text: What will you do if it rains?
just to be on the safe side
phrases.use: Explaining why you are being careful.
Giving the one condition that must be true.

phrases.text: I'll ring them as soon as I get home.
phrases.use: Promising to do something at the first chance.
Saying that something is not necessary.
Helping a stressed friend feel better.

items.meaning: A second plan that you use if your first plan fails.
items.example: If it rains, our plan B is the café by the park.

items.meaning: Something extra that you keep ready, in case the first one fails or is lost.
items.example: We booked the hall as a backup, in case it rains.

items.meaning: To happen as planned, or to start something that was planned.
items.example: If the weather is good, the party will go ahead in the park.

items.meaning: The place where an event happens, for example a party, a concert or a meeting.
items.example: We need a venue for about fifty people.

items.meaning: Happening or used outside, not in a building.
items.example: The town has a free outdoor concert every summer.

items.meaning: The amount of money that you have for something, and plan to spend.
items.example: Our budget for the party is £300.

items.meaning: Before the time when something happens.
items.example: Book the tickets in advance. They're cheaper.

items.meaning: Careful, so that you are ready if something goes wrong. People often say: just to be …
items.example: Take an umbrella, just to be on the safe side.

items.meaning: Something that might happen, but is not certain.
items.example: There's a possibility of rain on Saturday afternoon.

items.meaning: To tell someone what you think they should do.
items.example: The doctor advised me to rest for a week.

items.meaning: To tell someone about a danger or a problem before it happens.
items.example: I warned my neighbours that the party might be noisy.

items.meaning: Practical and careful, and based on good reasons.
items.example: Booking a room inside is a sensible idea.

items.meaning: A short, useful piece of advice.
items.example: Here's a tip: check the forecast the day before.

items.meaning: To deal with a difficult situation well enough.
items.example: It was a very busy week, but we coped.

items.meaning: Worried and tense, because you have too much to do or a problem to solve.
items.example: I always feel stressed before a big event.

sound.title: The rise in an if sentence
sound.explain: An if sentence has two halves. At the end of the first half, your voice goes up a little, because the sentence is not finished. At the end of the second half, it goes down. Listen to each one, then say it.
groups: If it rains · we'll use the café
As long as it's dry · we'll stay in the park
As soon as I get home · I'll ring them
lines: If it's dry, go ahead with the park.
If it looks bad, move to the café.
If I were you, I'd book a backup venue.

sayIt.instructions: Say Carlos's lines. Record yourself, then listen back. Does your voice go up at the end of the if half, and down at the end of the sentence?
lines: If I were you, I'd book a backup venue, just to be on the safe side. The café by the park has a big room upstairs.
They won't charge for the room as long as everyone orders food. But you should book it in advance. It gets busy at weekends.
Check the forecast on Friday. If it's dry, go ahead with the park. If it looks bad, move to the café.
No, you needn't do that. Ask everyone to bring something. You'll cope, don't worry.

spot.instructions: Look at these sentences from the conversation. The first three talk about plans that depend on something. The last two give advice.
examples: But what will you do if it rains?
They won't charge for the room as long as everyone orders food.
I'll ring the café as soon as I get home.
You ought to warn everyone that there's a possibility of a change.
spot.question: In the first three sentences, which half has will, and which half stays in the present? In the last two, which one says something is a good idea, and which one says it isn't necessary?
spot.answer: Will goes in the main half: what will you do, they won't charge, I'll ring. The half with if, as long as or as soon as stays in the present: rains, orders, get. Ought to says something is a good idea, like should. Needn't says it isn't necessary.

rules.title: If it rains, we'll …: plans that depend on something
rule: if + present, then will + verb: If it rains, we'll move to the café.
No will after if, unless, as long as or as soon as: I'll ring you as soon as I get home.
unless = if not: Unless it rains, we'll eat outside.
as long as = only if: They won't charge for the room as long as we order food.
as soon as = at the moment that: I'll decide as soon as I see the forecast.
rules.mistake: Not: If it will rain, we will move. Say: If it rains, we will move.

rules.title: Advice: should, ought to, needn't
rule: should + verb: You should book in advance. You shouldn't leave it too late.
ought to + verb means the same: You ought to warn people.
needn't + verb = it isn't necessary: You needn't buy all the food.
Friendly advice: If I were you, I'd book the café.
Asking for advice: What would you advise? Should I hire chairs?
rules.mistake: Not: You should to book. Not: You needn't to pay. Say: You should book. You needn't pay.

practice.q: If it ___ tomorrow, we'll have the party inside.
practice.why: There is no will after if: if it rains.

practice.q: I'll call you as soon as the bus ___ .
practice.why: There is no will after as soon as: the bus arrives.
Unless means if not: we'll eat outside if it doesn't rain.

practice.q: You can borrow my car ___ you bring it back by six.
practice.why: As long as means only if: bringing the car back by six is the condition.

practice.q: You ___ book the venue early. It gets very busy.
practice.why: Should + verb gives advice, with no to.

practice.q: You ought ___ warn your guests about the change.
practice.why: Ought always has to after it: ought to warn.

practice.q: You ___ bring any food. There's plenty.
If I ___ you, I'd take an umbrella.
practice.why: If I were you is the fixed phrase for friendly advice.

practice.q: What will you do if the venue ___ ?
practice.why: There is no will after if: if the venue is closed.

practice.q: Unless we ___ a cheaper venue, we can't stay within our budget.
practice.why: Unless already means if not, so don't is not needed.

yourTurn.prompt: Your friend is planning a picnic for their birthday next Sunday, and asks for your advice. Write four sentences: two with if or unless, one with should or ought to, and one with needn't.
yourTurn.model: If it rains, you can use my flat. Unless the weather is terrible, I'd still go to the park. You ought to check the forecast on Saturday evening. You needn't buy plates, because I've got lots.

text.title: Hire terms, and a repair card
text.type: Terms and conditions, and repair card
text.body:
PRACTICE DOCUMENT: this company does not exist.
FENMOOR PARTY HIRE
Tents · tables · chairs · lights
TERMS AND CONDITIONS
1. Please bring photo ID, for example a passport or a driving licence, when you collect your items.
2. All items are due back by 5 pm on the date on your booking form.
3. You can extend your hire as long as you tell us before 4 pm on the due date.
4. Unless items are back on time, we charge a late fee of £20 a day.
5. We return your £50 deposit as long as everything comes back clean and undamaged.
6. Please report any damage when you return the items. Otherwise, you will pay for a replacement.
7. To change or cancel a booking, please tell us in writing. An email is fine.

- - - - - - - -

PRACTICE CARD: this hall does not exist.
RIVERSIDE COMMUNITY HALL · REPAIR CARD
The lift is temporarily out of order after a breakdown on Monday. Please use the stairs.
How to report a fault
1. Fill in one card for each fault.
2. Mark the card URGENT only in an emergency: water, smoke or a person stuck in the lift.
3. Give the card to the person at the desk, and keep the yellow copy. It has your reference number.
What happens next
An engineer will check the fault as soon as the card reaches the office. If a new part is needed, the repair can take up to five working days.

gist.q: What is the first document for?
gist.a: the rules for hiring party equipment
wrong: the prices of tents and chairs
the rules for using the community hall
gist.why: It is the terms and conditions of a party hire company.

gist.q: Why is there a repair card at the hall?
gist.a: so that people can report a fault
wrong: so that people can book the hall
so that people can hire the lift
gist.why: The card tells you how to report a fault and what happens next.

detail.q: You want to keep the tent for one more day. What must you do?
detail.a: tell the company before 4 pm on the due date
wrong: bring it back and book it again
detail.why: Term 3 says you can extend your hire as long as you tell them before 4 pm on the due date.

detail.q: You bring the chairs back one day late. How much extra do you pay?
detail.why: Term 4 says there is a late fee of £20 a day.

detail.q: You break a table, but you don't tell the company. What happens?
detail.a: You pay for a new table.
detail.why: Term 6 says you must report damage, otherwise you pay for a replacement.

detail.q: When should you mark a repair card URGENT?
detail.a: only in an emergency, like smoke or water
wrong: whenever the lift is out of order
when you want a repair the same day
detail.why: The card says: Mark the card URGENT only in an emergency.

items.meaning: To pay money to use something for a short time.
items.example: We hired a tent and twenty chairs for the party.

items.meaning: The rules that you agree to when you buy, rent or use something.
items.example: Read the terms and conditions before you sign.

items.meaning: Expected or needed at a certain time.
items.example: The chairs are due back on Monday by 5 pm.

items.meaning: To make something last longer.
items.example: Can I extend the hire for one more day?

items.meaning: An amount of money that you pay for a service.
items.example: There's a late fee of £20 a day.

items.meaning: Written down, for example in a letter or an email, not only said.
items.example: Please send any changes in writing.

items.meaning: Not working. We usually say this about a machine.
items.example: The lift is out of order, so please use the stairs.

items.meaning: For a short time only, not for ever.
items.example: The café is temporarily closed for repairs.

items.meaning: A document that shows who you are, such as a passport or a driving licence.
items.example: Please bring photo ID when you collect the tent.

items.meaning: A time when a machine or a vehicle stops working.
items.example: We had a breakdown on the motorway and waited two hours for help.

model.title: My plan, and my plan B
model.body:
MY PLAN: SAMIR'S LEAVING PARTY
What: a picnic in Riverside Park
When: Saturday 14 June, 2 pm to 6 pm
Budget: £200
I've hired a tent, two tables and twenty chairs from Fenmoor Party Hire. They're due back by 5 pm on Monday, and I'll take my passport as ID when I collect them.
If it rains, we'll move to Riverside Community Hall. I've booked the small room, just to be on the safe side. I'll decide on Friday evening, as soon as I see the forecast.
If the lift at the hall is still out of order, I'll ask two friends to help me carry the food upstairs.
We'll get the deposit back as long as the tent comes back clean, so everyone will help me clean up at the end.

write.task: Write a plan for an event: a party, a trip or a meeting. It can be real or invented. Say what is arranged. Then write two things that could go wrong, and what you will do if they happen.
checklist: I said what the event is, where and when.
I wrote two things that could go wrong, with if or unless.
I used will only in the main half: If it rains, we'll …
I used as soon as, as long as or on the safe side once.

card.title: Plan A, plan B
card.situation: You are organising an event: a leaving party for a colleague, a family day out or a small outdoor concert. Your budget is £300. Your friend is planning an event too, and wants your opinion.
card.goal: Explain your plan and your plan B. Then listen to your friend's plan and give two pieces of advice with should, ought to, needn't or If I were you.

phrases: Unless we find a cheaper venue, we'll … .
prepare.notes: Make notes: the event, the venue, the date, your budget, and two things that could go wrong, with a plan B for each. Then think of one question to ask about your friend's plan.

doIt.liveClass: In the live class, tell a partner about your event and your plan B. Then your partner explains their plan, and you give advice. Change roles. Your teacher listens for will in the wrong half of the sentence.
doIt.wehel: You are my friend. First, ask me about the event I am planning: where, when, how much it costs, and what I will do if something goes wrong. Then tell me about a party you are planning, and ask for my advice. Use clear, simple English.

model.title: Two plans
lines: Priya
So, how's the planning going?
You
Quite well. It's a family day out at the lake on the twentieth. We're hiring a boat.
Priya
Lovely. What will you do if the weather's bad?
You
If it rains, we'll go to the museum in town instead. It's free, so it won't hurt our budget.
Priya
That's sensible. Have you booked the boat in advance?
You
Yes. And we can cancel for free as long as we tell them by Friday.
Priya
Great. I'm planning a small outdoor concert in my garden for the neighbours. But I'm worried about the noise.
You
If I were you, I'd warn the neighbours in advance. Or even better, invite them!
Priya
Good tip. Should I hire chairs?
You
No, you needn't hire chairs. People can bring their own. But you ought to have a plan B for rain.
Priya
Maybe the community hall?
You
Yes. Ring them as soon as you can. They get busy in the summer.
Priya
Thanks. I'll do it tonight.
compare: Did you say what your event is, where and when?
Did you give a plan B with if or unless?
Did you ask about your friend's plan: What will you do if …?
Did you give advice with should, ought to, needn't or If I were you?

I can make a plan B for an event.
I can give advice with should, ought to, needn't and If I were you.
I can read simple hire terms and a repair card.
I can write my plan, and what I will do if it goes wrong.

reading.before: Look at the title and the first page. What are the people planning? What do you think goes wrong?
reading.talk: Did the people in the story have a plan B? What would you advise them to do differently? Write three sentences with should or If I were you, or say them to Wehel.

quiz.q: If the café ___ full, we'll go to the park.
quiz.why: There is no will after if: if the café is full.

quiz.q: I'll send you the photos as soon as I ___ home.
quiz.why: There is no will after as soon as: as soon as I get home.

quiz.q: You can work from home on Fridays ___ you answer your phone.
quiz.why: As long as means only if: answering your phone is the condition.

quiz.q: You ___ bring anything. There's lots of food.
Take a coat, just to be on the ___ side.
quiz.why: To be on the safe side means to be careful, in case something goes wrong.

quiz.q: The place where a party or a meeting takes place is the ___ .
quiz.why: A venue is the place where an event happens.

quiz.q: The ticket machine isn't working. It's out of ___ .
quiz.why: Out of order means not working.

quiz.q: I ___ for this company for five years, and I still enjoy it.
quiz.why: For five years up to now, so we use the present perfect.

quiz.q: This is the flat ___ I lived when I first came to the city.
quiz.why: Where joins a sentence about a place.

quiz.q: I ___ home when I saw the accident.
quiz.why: The background action takes the past continuous: I was walking.

liveClass: Day 1: practise the party conversation in pairs. Then a chain: each learner answers What will you do if…? and asks the next learner a new one (if the train is late, if your phone breaks, if you win some money).

Day 2: an advice clinic. Each learner describes a small problem: a noisy neighbour, a party on a small budget, a stressful week. The others give advice with should, ought to, needn't and If I were you.
Day 3: the task. Learners plan an event with a budget and a plan B, explain it to a partner, then give advice about the partner's plan. Listen for will in the wrong half of the sentence.
Day 4: talk about the book and its plan B. Two learners read their plans aloud, and the class finds the weakest point in each plan and suggests a backup.
